ami_style_notes: The meeting has a casual, collegial video-call style with mostly short-to-medium turns during setup and discussion, shifting to long, structured monologues for presentations. Small overlaps, delayed responses, and fragmented audio-like phrasing are common, especially in greetings and transitions. Speakers use frequent fillers and hesitations—“um,” “yeah,” “okay,” “I mean,” repeated words, false starts, and self-corrections—and often hedge claims with phrases like “I think,” “sort of,” “maybe,” “likely,” or “we’re interested in.” Formality is moderate: introductions and talks are professional, but the surrounding chat is warm, joking, and informal. Questions are usually framed politely and tentatively, often prefaced with praise or disclaimers such as having a “quick” or “naive” question. Participants build on one another by restating part of a prior point before asking for clarification, while disagreement is indirect and exploratory rather than confrontational. Responses tend to acknowledge the question positively, admit uncertainty openly, and identify open questions rather than assert definitive conclusions.
research_problem: Understanding how urban green space affects mental health outcomes in low-income communities

speakers.name: Priya Nanduri
speakers.background: A computer scientist with 9 years of experience building mobile data-collection systems and applied statistical models for public-health and civic research. She has led projects involving GPS traces, app-based surveys, missing-data diagnostics, sampling weights, and fairness checks for predictive and explanatory models. For this study, she oversees the survey app, consent flow, data security, integration of neighborhood-level measures, and the analysis plan for the May 2027 pilot.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Priya treats the study design as a measurement and inference pipeline: who can access the app, what the phone records, which observations are missing, and how modeling choices affect estimated associations between green-space exposure and mental-health outcomes. She is attentive to systematic distortions introduced by device ownership, participation patterns, location accuracy, question wording, and model specification, while relying on Mateo and Lin to establish the social and ecological validity of the variables.
speakers.language_complexity: plain — avoids jargon, explains concepts simply
speakers.epistemic_stance: defers to other experts outside their domain

speakers.name: Mateo Alvarez
speakers.background: A sociology postdoctoral researcher with 5 years of experience conducting mixed-methods research on neighborhood inequality, housing insecurity, public-space governance, and health. His work combines semi-structured interviews, community-based recruitment, survey interpretation, and qualitative coding, often in partnership with tenant groups and local nonprofits. He will lead resident and organization interviews and advise on recruitment, questionnaire wording, and interpretation of reported park access and use.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Mateo approaches green space as a socially governed resource rather than a neutral physical amenity. He expects access, comfort, safety, and use to be shaped by race, class, immigration status, policing, disability, work schedules, and residents' prior experiences with public institutions. He focuses on how recruitment practices, interviewer assumptions, and institutional narratives may affect whose accounts are heard and how residents are represented.
speakers.language_complexity: moderate — balances jargon with accessible language
speakers.epistemic_stance: highly confident in their discipline's contribution

speakers.name: Lin Chen
speakers.background: An urban ecologist and principal investigator with 14 years of experience studying how vegetation structure, heat exposure, maintenance regimes, and biodiversity vary across cities. She has coordinated field audits of parks, street-tree corridors, and vacant-lot greening projects using standardized observation protocols, canopy measurements, photographic records, and GIS-based site inventories. She will coordinate repeated field observations across the three neighborhoods before and during the May 2027 pilot.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Lin distinguishes the presence of greenery from the ecological and usable qualities of a green space. She wants observations to capture canopy cover, shade, vegetation condition, species composition, maintenance, seating, permeability, noise, and the difference between a mapped park and a space residents can actually occupy. She is careful not to infer residents' mental-health experiences from ecological indicators alone and looks to the social-science and computing teams to connect site conditions to lived exposure and reported outcomes.
speakers.language_complexity: moderate — balances jargon with accessible language
speakers.epistemic_stance: defers to other experts outside their domain

seed_spec.explicit_instruction: Generate a natural planning-meeting transcript. Priya (computer science) and Mateo (sociology) must each use the term "bias" while discussing the study design, but they must use it in their discipline-specific senses. Priya knows and explains bias as systematic error in data, measurement, sampling, or model outputs that can distort estimates or predictions. Mateo knows and explains bias as socially patterned prejudice, unequal treatment, or assumptions affecting how people are perceived, recruited, questioned, or represented. Lin may participate in the broader discussion but must not provide an additional discipline-specific definition of "bias." The participants should discuss ordinary study-planning details, including the May 2027 pilot, recruitment, the mobile survey, interviews, and field observations. The different meanings should emerge clearly from the conversation without anyone explicitly announcing that this is a jargon test. Do not resolve the two meanings into a single definition; preserve the moment in which the shared word has discipline-specific meanings.

transcript.speaker: Lin Chen
transcript.text: Hi, everyone—can you hear me okay? Great. Um, I thought today we could get the spatial unit and the basic measures aligned before we get too far into the pilot logistics. For the field side especially, I need to know whether I’m auditing parks and lots as sites, street segments, or actual walking routes, because canopy on a map can look quite, quite different from the shade and access somebody encounters.

transcript.speaker: Mateo Alvarez
transcript.text: I’d be wary of making the site the only unit. In the early conversations, people described the same park very differently depending on when they could go and the route there, especially after work or with kids. Could the audit distinguish the site itself from the approach route, and maybe capture time-of-day conditions rather than- rather than treating accessibility as fixed?

transcript.speaker: Priya Nanduri
transcript.text: For the app, I’d avoid making one GPS point stand in for access. We can link a reported visit to a site or route category, but I want to ask a short follow-up about when they went and whether they walked there, because otherwise a missed boundary could look like a bad report. Lin, could your audit give us separate fields for the approach route and the site- the space itself?

transcript.speaker: Mateo Alvarez
transcript.text: Mm, yeah.

transcript.speaker: Lin Chen
transcript.text: I can split it that way. A site sheet for the park or lot, then a short approach-segment sheet for the likely walking entry. I'd want the approach tied to the route category Priya is using, though, because otherwise we could audit a pleasant block that nobody, nobody actually takes. And we should probably do at least some late-afternoon repeats. The canopy cover alone really missed the walking-side shade in the walkthroughs.

transcript.speaker: Priya Nanduri
transcript.text: That works. I can have the app's visit prompt use a broad route category instead of acting like we know their exact path, and then link it to the matching approach audit. Lin, for those late-afternoon repeats, how stable do you expect the conditions to be from week to week? I need to know if one score can reasonably sit alongside responses collected across the whole pilot.

transcript.speaker: Lin Chen
transcript.text: The structural features should be pretty stable over a few weeks, like path surface, gate status, seating, and major vegetation condition, so those can have a baseline score. But shade, noise, litter, and whether the space feels occupiable can shift by hour and maintenance cycle. I'd keep those as dated observation fields rather than collapsing them into one number. I'm less sure we can safely get enough evening observations to treat those as systematic. Actually, we'd need to check staffing first.

transcript.speaker: Priya Nanduri
transcript.text: That distinction helps. I can keep the audit date and time in the linkage, so we don't imply somebody's response saw conditions from a different week. And for the baseline fields, we can use the stable score. Maybe for the pilot, we treat evening observations as a coverage question first, like how many sites and weeks we can actually observe. I was going to say build a full time-of-day measure, but not around them yet.

transcript.speaker: Lin Chen
transcript.text: I can treat evening as a small stratified set for the pilot, enough to see whether the day-versus-evening difference is large and whether staff can do it safely, but not enough to claim full coverage. Mateo, when people say a place is unusable after work, do they usually mean the route, the gate or programming, or something else? That would help me decide what to flag in those, those repeats.

transcript.speaker: Mateo Alvarez
transcript.text: It’s usually a bundle, and it varies by person. Gate hours or poor lighting, sure, but also whether someone expects to be questioned, feels watched, or can only go with children after a long shift. I’d flag those, but I’d be careful not to make a daytime observer’s inference about who belongs there into an audit variable. That’s a place bias can creep in. The interviews can help us interpret what the evening repeats don’t...

transcript.speaker: Priya Nanduri
transcript.text: That’s a useful boundary for the app too. We shouldn’t infer felt safety or belonging from whether someone did or didn’t visit, because that would bake observer and participation bias into the exposure measure. Mateo, in the interviews, have people said whether they’d answer a quick phone prompt while they’re out or later at home? That affects what recall window we can reasonably use.

transcript.speaker: Mateo Alvarez
transcript.text: A few people said they'd answer later, not while they were in the space, especially if they were with children, commuting, or worried about drawing attention to themselves. I think a same-evening prompt with a next-day fallback might be less burdensome than trying to catch the visit in real time. But I'd want to ask directly in the first interviews. The people willing to use the app may not be the- may not be the ones for whom an in-the-moment prompt is hardest.

transcript.speaker: Lin Chen
transcript.text: Hm, that makes sense.

transcript.speaker: Priya Nanduri
transcript.text: I think we should design for that, rather than treat a delayed response as a failure. We could do a same-evening notification, then a next-day recall prompt that asks about the most recent visit and roughly when it happened. But I want to keep a clear timestamp for when they answered, or rather, when they answered versus when they say the visit occurred, so we can see whether recall is changing the reports.

transcript.speaker: Mateo Alvarez
transcript.text: Yeah, and the fallback needs an explicit option for no visit, but it can't read like disinterest. Maybe it asks what, um, got in the way, like time, getting there, physical access, not feeling comfortable, or something else, with multiple selections and a skip, since those reasons can overlap.

transcript.speaker: Priya Nanduri
transcript.text: And for the analysis, I’d keep that as a separate barrier outcome. I wouldn’t fold it into “non-use.” Multiple selections and skip matter, otherwise we’ll mistake a missing answer or a complicated evening for a preference. We should also log whether the fallback was answered that same evening or the next day, since those groups may not be comparable.

transcript.speaker: Mateo Alvarez
transcript.text: Before we settle the app flow, Priya, can I ask what it requires up front? Location permission, a smartphone with data, account creation, anything like that? I'm worried the people most likely to use the next-day option may also be the ones screened out or, um, dropping off before we ever see that barrier question.

transcript.speaker: Priya Nanduri
transcript.text: We should not require location permission, a data plan, or account creation just to enroll and answer the core survey. The app can work with a study code and store responses offline until it connects. Location would be an optional, separate consent, and I need to confirm with security whether a coarser, coarser location setting still lets us calculate the distance categories we need. For the pilot, I'll make a participation funnel so we can see exactly where people are excluded or drop off.

transcript.speaker: Mateo Alvarez
transcript.text: That’s reassuring. Can the funnel distinguish people who decline optional location from people who never finish enrollment or who stop responding later? Those are socially different processes. And I’d also want to see how the study-code setup lands with the community organizations, whether it feels independent enough that residents don’t connect participation to services or eligibility...

transcript.speaker: Priya Nanduri
transcript.text: Absolutely. I’ll separate consented-but-no-location, enrollment not completed, and later survey attrition, instead of using one overall completion rate. And on the study code, I’d like Mateo’s read from the organizations before we finalize the language, because technically simple can still feel like it’s— tied to a service provider.

transcript.speaker: Mateo Alvarez
transcript.text: Yeah, I’ll raise it with them as a question about perceived independence, not just whether they’ll distribute a link. I’m particularly interested in whether recruitment through a tenant group versus, say, a service provider changes who feels safe declining or participating—and we may need more than one channel if it does.

transcript.speaker: Priya Nanduri
transcript.text: That matters for the funnel too. We should tag the recruitment channel without making it identifiable, so we can see whether consent, location opt-in, and follow-up differ by channel. The pilot probably needs to test at least two channels in each neighborhood. Otherwise, if response is low- if we only use one channel, we won’t know whether it’s the app or who we reached.

transcript.speaker: Mateo Alvarez
transcript.text: Two channels per neighborhood feels like the minimum. I’d want the scripts documented too, and who delivers them. A tenant-group invitation and a provider invitation can lead to different consent patterns, even with the same link, and that’s not just a recruitment nuisance. It shapes whose park experiences we’re able to interpret.

transcript.speaker: Priya Nanduri
transcript.text: Yeah, we can record channel, inviter type, and script version as separate, non-identifying fields. Then the pilot summaries can show where patterns diverge—who starts, who opts into location, who answers the fallback—without pretending recruitment channel is random. I’d rather see that early than pool everybody and call the differences neighborhood effects.

transcript.speaker: Lin Chen
transcript.text: And it’ll help us keep recruitment effects separate from neighborhood differences in the exposure data.

transcript.speaker: Priya Nanduri
transcript.text: I think we’ve covered what I needed for today. I’ll carry this into the pilot flow, and we can pick up the open pieces next time. Thanks, both.

transcript.speaker: Mateo Alvarez
transcript.text: All right, take care, both.

transcript.speaker: Lin Chen
transcript.text: Thanks—bye, both.
